title: Hangover Kit Ideas: What to Pack for Basic, Deluxe, and Party Kits
excerpt: How to build a hangover kit that actually helps: three tiers (basic, deluxe gift, and group kits for weddings and bachelorette weekends), what goes in each, what to leave out, and what the evidence says about DHM, electrolytes, and B vitamins.
metaDescription: Hangover kit ideas for yourself, a gift, or a bachelorette/wedding group: what to pack, what to skip, and what the evidence says on DHM and electrolytes.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short list first:** a good hangover kit is mostly water, electrolytes, something gentle to eat, and a plan for sleep. Those four things do most of the work, and they cost very little. Supplements like DHM (dihydromyricetin) and B vitamins are optional add-ons, not the core. A painkiller can go in for the morning headache, but it needs clear labeling and a note about alcohol. Everything else is comfort and presentation.

This guide walks through three kit tiers (a basic kit for yourself, a deluxe kit as a gift, and a group kit for weddings, bachelorette weekends, and trips), what goes in each one and why, what to leave out, and how to keep it honest and safe. We also cover what the research does and doesn't say about each item, because a lot of "hangover kit" lists online are mostly marketing.

> **This is not medical advice.** A hangover kit can make a rough morning more comfortable. It can't make heavy drinking safe, and nothing in it treats alcohol poisoning. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin. Don't leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off." If you take prescription medicines, are pregnant, or have liver, kidney, or heart conditions, check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding painkillers or supplements to your own kit.

## What a Hangover Kit Actually Needs to Do

Before picking items, it helps to know what a hangover is. Researchers still don't agree on a single cause, but the main contributors are fairly well understood:

- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. You pee more than you drink, and you wake up short on fluid and salts.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. A lot of next-day misery is plain sleep deprivation.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which is behind the nausea and the "can't face food" feeling.
- **Inflammation and by-products.** Your body breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and drinking triggers an inflammatory response. Both are linked to headache, fatigue, and that general poisoned feeling.
- **Low blood sugar and skipped meals.** Drinking can lower blood sugar, especially if you didn't eat much.

A useful kit targets the problems you can actually do something about: fluids and salts, the stomach, sleep, and the headache. That's the whole design brief. If an item doesn't help with one of those, it's decoration (which is fine in a gift, as long as nobody pretends it's medicine).

One honest caveat up front. Systematic reviews of hangover remedies, including a 2005 review in the *BMJ* and a larger 2022 review in the journal *Addiction*, found that the evidence for nearly every hangover product is weak, based on small studies. The only reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. A kit helps you recover a bit more comfortably. It doesn't undo a heavy night.

## The Core Items (Every Tier Gets These)

These are the items that earn a spot in every kit, from the cheapest to the most elaborate.

### 1. Water, and a way to drink it

A refillable bottle sounds too obvious to list, but it's the item people forget. Plain water before bed and in the morning is the foundation. In a gift kit, a reusable bottle doubles as the container and the thing people actually keep.

### 2. Electrolytes

Because alcohol makes you lose salts as well as water, an electrolyte drink or powder usually beats plain water for a hangover morning. The key ingredients are sodium and potassium, with a little sugar to help absorption. Your options:

- **Oral rehydration solutions** like Pedialyte or store-brand equivalents. These have more sodium and less sugar than sports drinks. They're designed for fluid loss from illness, but they suit a hangover morning well.
- **Electrolyte powder sticks.** Light, cheap, and easy to pack. Best for travel kits and group kits because they fit in an envelope.
- **Sports drinks** like Gatorade. Fine if that's what you'll actually drink, though they carry more sugar and less sodium than oral rehydration drinks.

We compare the two most common options in detail in [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover). The short version for kit-building: powder sticks for portability, a ready-to-drink bottle for the "morning after" gift where nobody wants to mix anything.

### 3. Something gentle to eat

Bland, easy food helps with low blood sugar and an unsettled stomach. Good options that keep well:

- Saltine crackers or pretzels (salt plus easy carbs)
- Plain granola bars or oat bars
- Instant oatmeal cups
- Bananas, if the kit will be used within a day or two (potassium plus easy carbs)
- Instant broth or bouillon cubes (salt and warm fluid, easy on the stomach)

Skip greasy snacks. The idea that a greasy breakfast "soaks up" alcohol the next morning isn't supported. By then the alcohol has already been absorbed, and fatty food can make nausea worse for some people.

### 4. Something for the stomach

- **Ginger chews or ginger tea.** Ginger has reasonable evidence for nausea in general (mostly from pregnancy and motion-sickness research), though it hasn't been well studied for hangovers specifically. It's cheap, safe for most people, and a nice kit item.
- **Antacid tablets** (calcium carbonate types). They can help with heartburn and acid after drinking.
- A note on **Pepto-Bismol**: it's popular for an upset stomach, but it contains a salicylate (an aspirin relative), so it shouldn't be combined with aspirin, and people on blood thinners or with aspirin allergies should avoid it. If you include it in a gift kit, include the box with the label, not loose tablets.

### 5. A sleep kit

Since poor sleep drives so much of a hangover, sleep items are some of the most useful things in a kit:

- An eye mask
- Foam earplugs
- A "do not disturb" sign for hotel kits (a fun custom item for group trips)

Avoid adding sleep medicines. Sedating products, including over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aids, should not be combined with alcohol, because the drowsiness stacks up in ways that can be dangerous.

## Painkillers: Include Them Carefully, or Not at All

A headache remedy is what most people expect in a hangover kit. It's also the item that needs the most care, especially in a kit you're handing to someone else.

- **Ibuprofen or naproxen (NSAIDs)** are generally the more common choice for a hangover headache. They're easier on the liver, but harder on the stomach, and their US labels warn about stomach bleeding risk for people who have three or more drinks a day. They're best taken with food and water, in the morning, once you're up.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is processed by the liver, the same organ dealing with alcohol. One normal dose the morning after a moderate night is unlikely to hurt a healthy adult, but it should never be taken before bed "just in case," and heavy regular drinkers should ask a doctor first. We explain the liver chemistry in [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).
- **Aspirin** irritates the stomach and thins the blood. It's the weakest choice for a hangover kit.

**Our advice for gift and group kits:** if you include a painkiller, use small sealed single-dose packets with the original label and dosing information, and add a card that says "take in the morning with food, not before bed, and not with other products that contain the same medicine." Don't pour loose pills into bags. Many people prefer to leave painkillers out of group kits entirely and let guests use their own, which avoids questions about allergies, medications, and pregnancy. That's a perfectly good choice.

## DHM, B Vitamins, and Other Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Supplements are optional, and they're also where most of the overselling happens. Here's a straight look at the ones that commonly show up in kits.

### DHM (dihydromyricetin)

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), used in traditional East Asian hangover remedies. The best-known research is a 2012 study in *The Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues, which found that DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal in rats, apparently by acting on GABA-A receptors in the brain. Lab and animal studies also suggest effects on how the liver processes alcohol and its by-products.

What's missing is strong human evidence for hangovers specifically. There are only small human studies, and they are not enough to say how much DHM helps people the morning after. So we'd describe it as promising, plausible, and popular, not proven. It's reasonable to include in a kit for someone who wants to try it, as long as the card doesn't promise results.

Practical notes for kits:

- Most people take DHM while drinking or before bed, not the next morning. Put a simple card in the kit that says so, or link to our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025).
- Keep it in its original sealed container or blister pack with the label.
- DHM can interact with some medicines. Anyone on prescription drugs should check with a pharmacist first.

If you want to add DHM, these are the products we track and review:

- **For a deluxe single gift:** [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) pairs 1,000 mg of DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, a B-complex, and electrolytes, which covers several kit categories in one product. It's the priciest per serving (about $1.93) and has 15 servings per pack.
- **For splitting across a group kit:** [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is plain DHM at 1,000 mg per serving and about $0.80 a serving, with 30 servings per bottle. It's the budget pick if you're building kits for a lot of people, though single-ingredient means you'll want electrolytes and B vitamins separately.
- **For a small, travel-friendly add-on:** [Flyby Recovery](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CCK34H46?tag=dhmguide-20) is a lower-dose DHM (300 mg) blend with milk thistle, B vitamins, and electrolytes. It comes in small packs, which suit a weekend bag but make it a costly choice per serving.
- **For someone who wants a liver-focused blend:** [Toniiq Ease](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07S448GTT?tag=dhmguide-20) combines a lower dose of DHM with reishi mushroom and milk thistle, at around $0.62 a serving.

For a full comparison of brands, doses, and prices, see our [supplement reviews](/reviews).

### B vitamins

Heavy drinking can lower levels of several B vitamins over time, especially thiamine (B1), which is why doctors give thiamine to people with alcohol use disorder. For a single night out in a well-nourished person, the case is weaker. There's some limited research linking higher dietary intake of certain B vitamins to milder hangovers, but it's observational and not conclusive. A B-complex is inexpensive and generally safe at label doses, so it's a fine kit add-on, just not a centerpiece. Several DHM blends already include B vitamins, so check labels before you double up.

### Things we'd leave out or downplay

- **"Detox" teas and drinks.** Your liver and kidneys do the detoxing. Products that claim to "flush" alcohol overpromise.
- **Activated charcoal.** It barely binds alcohol, and it can interfere with medicines. Not useful here.
- **Prescription anti-nausea drugs.** These are prescription-only for a reason, and they don't belong in a gift bag.
- **Energy shots and lots of caffeine.** A coffee is fine for many people, but big doses of caffeine on a dehydrated, shaky morning can make you feel worse.

For a broader look at which supplements have any evidence behind them, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## Tier 1: The Basic Hangover Kit (For Yourself)

This is the kit to keep in a drawer or a weekend bag. It's cheap, it covers the essentials, and you can build it in one grocery run. Expect to spend roughly $15 to $30, depending on what you already have.

| Item | Why it's in |
|---|---|
| Reusable water bottle | Fluids before bed and in the morning |
| 4 to 6 electrolyte powder sticks | Replaces lost salts and fluid |
| Saltine crackers or pretzels | Easy carbs and salt for an upset stomach |
| Ginger chews | Mild help with nausea |
| Antacid tablets | Heartburn and acid |
| Ibuprofen (in its labeled bottle) | Morning headache, taken with food |
| Eye mask and earplugs | Protects the sleep you get |

**How to use it:** drink a glass of water with an electrolyte stick before bed, put the bottle on the nightstand, and save the painkiller for the morning after you've eaten something. If you take DHM, that also goes in before bed or during the evening, not the next day.

The basic kit is also the right answer for most people who are thinking about a kit at all. If you drink occasionally and want to feel a bit better, this covers it. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter more than any kit: pacing, eating beforehand, and alternating drinks with water.

## Tier 2: The Deluxe Hangover Kit (A Gift for One Person)

The deluxe kit is the "thoughtful gift" version: a birthday, a 21st, a friend's big night, or a care package for someone who's traveling. It has the basics, better presentation, and a few comfort upgrades. Expect roughly $40 to $80, mostly depending on the container and whether you include a supplement.

**Container ideas:** a zip-up toiletry bag, a small insulated cooler bag, a canvas tote, or a nice tin. A toiletry bag is the most practical, since people actually reuse it.

**What goes in:**

- Everything from the basic kit
- A ready-to-drink oral rehydration drink, so there's nothing to mix
- Instant oatmeal or broth cups
- Ginger tea bags or a small jar of honey
- A quality sleep mask (silk or contoured)
- Lip balm and a travel-size face wipe pack (dry lips and a gross morning face are real hangover complaints)
- Mint gum or breath strips
- A DHM product, if the person is open to supplements (see the options above)
- A small card with simple instructions

**The instruction card** is the most useful upgrade, and it costs nothing. Something like this works well:

> *Tonight: water and an electrolyte drink before bed. DHM, if you're taking it, during the night or before sleep. Tomorrow: eat something gentle first, then the painkiller if you need it, with food. More electrolytes through the morning. Sleep in if you can.*

That card does more for the person than any product in the bag, because it puts things in the right order.

## Tier 3: The Group Kit for Weddings, Bachelorette Parties, and Trips

Group kits are where hangover kits have become a real trend: welcome bags at destination weddings, bachelorette and bachelor weekend bags, festival group packs, and "recovery stations" at the morning-after brunch. The goal shifts from one person's comfort to giving a lot of people a few useful basics, safely and affordably.

### What works well in a group kit

- **Electrolyte powder sticks** (two per person). The single most useful group item: light, cheap, and nobody worries about allergies.
- **A bottle of water**, ideally custom-labeled for the event
- **Crackers or a granola bar**
- **Ginger chews** or mints
- **Earplugs and an eye mask**, especially for hotel rooms and shared houses
- **Lip balm and hair ties** (small, cheap, always needed)
- **A short schedule card** with the next day's brunch time and a reminder to hydrate

### What to be careful with in group kits

- **Painkillers.** You don't know everyone's allergies, medications, pregnancy status, or health conditions. If you include them, use sealed, labeled single-dose packets, never loose pills. Many planners leave them out and put a labeled bottle at a central spot for guests who want one.
- **Supplements, including DHM.** Same logic. Some guests take medications that could interact, and some won't want them. If you include DHM, put it in sealed, labeled packaging with a note to check with a pharmacist if they take any prescription medicine. Buying one larger bottle, like [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and keeping it at a "recovery station" with the label visible is often cleaner than splitting pills into bags.
- **Anything that implies drinking more is fine.** A kit is a nice gesture. Joke cards are fun, but steer clear of messaging like "drink all you want, this has you covered."

### The bachelorette (and bachelor) angle

Bachelorette weekends tend to involve several nights of drinking back to back, often with travel, late nights, and not much real food. That makes the basics matter more, not less:

- **Pack for multiple mornings.** Two or three electrolyte sticks per person per night, not one for the whole weekend.
- **Prioritize sleep items.** Shared rooms and late nights are the norm. Earplugs and eye masks cost very little and protect the one thing a multi-night weekend runs short on.
- **Plan food into the itinerary.** A real dinner before going out and a planned brunch do more than anything in the bag. Put the brunch time on the card.
- **Think about the bride or groom.** If they have a big event soon after, a calmer final night is a better gift than any kit.
- **Add a group safety note.** A buddy system, a shared ride plan, and the rule that nobody gets left alone if they've had too much. This is the most important thing a group kit can carry, and it fits on the back of the schedule card.

### Wedding welcome bags

For destination weddings, a "recovery" bag in the hotel room is a thoughtful touch, often handed out at check-in. Keep it simple and inclusive, since guests range from non-drinkers to grandparents: water, electrolytes, a local snack, a sleep mask, and a schedule. Calling it a "welcome" or "recovery" bag rather than a "hangover" kit keeps it appropriate for everyone. Put supplements and painkillers in a separate, clearly labeled basket at the front desk or brunch rather than in every bag.

### Rough budget for group kits

Group kit prices depend heavily on the container and custom printing. A practical bag with water, two electrolyte sticks, a snack, ginger chews, earplugs, and a printed card typically lands somewhere around $8 to $15 per person when bought in bulk. Custom bags, labels, and bigger containers push that up quickly. Electrolyte sticks and snacks are the easy places to save, since bulk packs are cheap.

## Festival and Travel Kits

Festivals and travel add heat, walking, crowds, and time zone changes to drinking. That raises the stakes on fluids and sleep:

- **More electrolytes than you think.** Heat and sweat add to the fluid loss from alcohol.
- **Sunscreen and a hat** belong in a festival kit, because sunburn and heat exhaustion feel a lot like a hangover and make it worse.
- **Check the rules.** Many festivals and airlines restrict what you can bring in (liquids, unlabeled pills). Keep medicines and supplements in their original labeled containers.

We go deeper on these situations in our [music festival survival guide](/never-hungover/music-festival-survival-dhm-2025).

## Mistakes to Avoid When Building a Kit

- **Loose, unlabeled pills.** This is the big one. Keep every medicine and supplement in its original labeled container or a sealed, labeled packet.
- **Doubling up on the same medicine.** Some "hangover relief" and cold products already contain acetaminophen or aspirin. Adding another painkiller on top can push someone over the safe limit without them realizing.
- **Including sleep aids.** Don't combine sedatives with alcohol.
- **Promising too much.** Cards that say a product "prevents hangovers" are both inaccurate and a little risky, because they can encourage people to drink more. "Helps you feel a bit better" is the honest framing.
- **Forgetting the non-drinkers.** In group settings, make kits that are still useful (water, snacks, sleep mask) to someone who isn't drinking.
- **Treating the kit as a safety net.** It isn't one. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, call for help.

## What Matters More Than the Kit

Here's the uncomfortable truth about hangover kits: the biggest factors are decided before the kit comes out of the bag. How much you drink, how fast, whether you ate, and how much sleep you get will outweigh any combination of products.

A few habits that do more than any item:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Alternate each drink with water.** It slows your pace and helps with fluid loss.
- **Set a limit before you start** and count drinks.
- **Choose drinks with fewer congeners.** Clear spirits tend to cause milder hangovers than dark spirits for many people, though the total amount still matters most.
- **Protect your sleep.** Plan the next morning so you can sleep in when possible.

If you want a deeper look at drinks to choose, see our guide to the [least hangover alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked), and for supplement timing, see [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking). For drinks that help on the morning after, see our roundup of [hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

## The Bottom Line

- The best hangover kits are built around four things: **fluids, electrolytes, gentle food, and sleep.** Those are cheap and genuinely useful.
- **DHM and B vitamins** are reasonable optional add-ons with promising but limited evidence. Include them honestly, in labeled packaging, with a note on timing.
- **Painkillers** need the most care. Ibuprofen in the morning with food is the usual choice. Never take acetaminophen before bed after drinking, and use sealed, labeled single doses in any kit you give away.
- **Group kits** for weddings and bachelorette weekends should focus on electrolytes, water, snacks, and sleep items, with supplements and medicines kept separate and clearly labeled.
- A kit makes a rough morning more comfortable. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe, and it's never a substitute for getting help when someone has had far too much.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What should be in a hangover kit?**

The core items are a water bottle, electrolyte powder or an oral rehydration drink, a gentle snack like crackers, something for the stomach such as ginger chews or antacids, and sleep items like an eye mask and earplugs. A painkiller such as ibuprofen can be added for the morning headache, kept in its labeled packaging. DHM and B vitamins are optional extras with limited evidence.

**What's a good hangover kit for a bachelorette party?**

Focus on electrolyte sticks (two or three per person per night), bottled water, crackers or granola bars, ginger chews, earplugs, eye masks, lip balm, and a card with the brunch time and a buddy-system reminder. Keep painkillers and supplements out of individual bags, or use sealed, labeled single-dose packets, because you won't know everyone's medications or allergies.

**Should I put DHM in a hangover kit?**

You can, as an optional item for people who want to try it. Animal and lab studies are promising, but human evidence for hangovers is limited, so don't promise results. Keep it in its original labeled packaging, include a note that it's usually taken during the evening or before bed rather than the next morning, and suggest that anyone on prescription medicine checks with a pharmacist first.

**Is it safe to put painkillers in a hangover kit?**

It can be, with care. Use sealed, labeled single-dose packets rather than loose pills, and include a note to take them in the morning with food and not combine them with other products containing the same medicine. Acetaminophen should never be taken before bed after drinking, and NSAIDs like ibuprofen can irritate the stomach. For group kits, many hosts leave painkillers out and keep a labeled bottle in a central place instead.

**Is Pedialyte or Gatorade better for a hangover kit?**

Oral rehydration drinks like Pedialyte have more sodium and less sugar, which suits fluid loss well. Sports drinks are fine if that's what someone will actually drink. For kits, electrolyte powder sticks are usually the most practical because they're light and cheap. See our full Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison for the details.

**How much does it cost to make a hangover kit?**

A basic kit for yourself is roughly $15 to $30. A deluxe gift kit with a nicer container and a supplement is roughly $40 to $80. Group kits for weddings or bachelorette parties usually land around $8 to $15 per person when bought in bulk, more with custom printing.

**Do B vitamins help with hangovers?**

The evidence is limited. Heavy drinking can lower B vitamin levels over time, and some observational research has linked higher B vitamin intake to milder hangovers, but that doesn't prove they help after a single night. A B-complex is inexpensive and generally safe at label doses, so it's a reasonable optional add-on, but it isn't a core kit item.

**Can a hangover kit prevent a hangover?**

No. A kit can make the morning more comfortable by replacing fluids, settling your stomach, and protecting your sleep, but the only reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. Eating beforehand, pacing yourself, and alternating drinks with water matter more than anything in the bag.
